figures.title: The Carbohydrate Family Tree
figures.subtitle: Sugars, starch and fiber, and how they show up on a label.

segments.name: What Carbohydrates Are
segments.text: Carbohydrates are the third energy-giving macronutrient, after fat and protein. Every gram you digest gives about four calories, the same as protein. They're your body's quickest fuel, and the brain and red blood cells depend on the glucose they supply.
segments.cue: Title, then the Carbohydrate box at the top

segments.name: Sugars
segments.text: On the left are the sugars: small carbohydrates with one or two units. Single sugars like glucose, fructose and galactose are the building blocks. Double sugars like table sugar and milk sugar are two of them joined. Below them are sugar alcohols, made from sugars, and added sugars, the ones put in during cooking or manufacturing.
segments.cue: Left branch: Sugars, Single sugars and Double sugars; then the dashed related group below: Sugar alcohols (dotted made-from arrow) and Added sugars

segments.name: Starch
segments.text: In the middle is starch: long chains of glucose that plants use to store energy. It comes in a straight form, amylose, and a branched form, amylopectin. Some starch escapes digestion and acts like fiber; that's resistant starch. Your own body stores glucose in a very branched form called glycogen.
segments.cue: Middle branch: Starch, Amylose (straight), Amylopectin (branched), Resistant; then the dashed digestion arrow down to Glucose, stored as Glycogen in the in-your-body frame

segments.name: Fiber
segments.text: On the right is fiber: carbohydrate your own enzymes can't break down. Soluble fiber dissolves into a gel; insoluble fiber adds bulk. Both are still important, as we'll see. Each box links to the figure that explains it.

segments.name: On the Label
segments.text: On a nutrition label, Total Carbohydrate includes all of these: starch, sugars, fiber and sugar alcohols. Dietary fiber and total sugars are listed inside it, and added sugars inside total sugars. The Daily Values are 275 grams for total carbohydrate, 28 for fiber and 50 for added sugars.
segments.cue: The three boxes under the tree

figures.title: From Atoms to a Sugar
figures.subtitle: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; a six-carbon chain that closes into a ring.

segments.name: Three Kinds of Atom
segments.text: Carbohydrates are built from just three kinds of atom. Carbon makes four bonds, like methane. Oxygen makes two, like water. Hydrogen makes one. Unlike protein, there's no nitrogen.

segments.name: Hydrated Carbon
segments.text: Many carbohydrates have the formula C n H 2 O n: one carbon for every water's worth of hydrogen and oxygen. That's where the name comes from, carbo-hydrate, hydrated carbon. There's no actual water inside; the atoms are just in that ratio. Glucose is C6H12O6.

segments.name: Glucose as a Chain
segments.text: Here's glucose drawn as a chain of six carbons. Carbon one, on the left, carries a C double bond O: that's the reactive end. Carbons two to five each carry an OH group, and carbon six on the right is a CH2OH. All those OH groups are why sugar dissolves so easily and tastes sweet.

notes.heading: Why the OH groups taste sweet
notes.text: Why the OH groups taste sweet: your sweet receptor, a protein pair called T1R2 and T1R3, has a pocket lined with charged amino acids. Sugar's OH groups form hydrogen bonds with them, the pocket closes around the sugar, and the receptor signals sweet. The spacing of neighbouring OH groups is what makes the fit work.

segments.name: Closing the Ring
segments.text: In water, the chain bends round and the oxygen of the OH on carbon five attacks carbon one. That oxygen becomes part of a ring with five carbons, and carbon one's old C double bond O turns into a new OH. Nothing is added or lost; it's still C6H12O6.

segments.name: Drawn in 3D
segments.text: More than ninety-nine percent of glucose is in the ring form at any moment. The rings on this page are drawn as 3D models, tilted so you can see which groups point up and which point down, because that turns out to matter a great deal.

figures.title: The Single Sugars
figures.subtitle: Glucose, galactose and fructose: same formula, different shapes.

segments.name: Alpha and Beta
segments.text: When the ring closes, the new OH on carbon one can point either way. Pointing down, below the ring, it's alpha-glucose; pointing out to the side, it's beta-glucose. In water they keep switching, about one third alpha and two thirds beta. Once glucose is locked into a chain, the choice is fixed, and that one direction decides whether you can digest it.

segments.name: Glucose
segments.text: Glucose is the main sugar in your blood and the fuel every cell can use. Your brain alone uses roughly a hundred and twenty grams a day. If you eat little carbohydrate, your liver makes glucose from protein and from the glycerol part of fats. Blood glucose that stays high, as in diabetes, damages blood vessels, nerves, kidneys and eyes over time. You find it free in fruit and honey, and as starch in grains, potatoes and beans.

segments.name: Galactose
segments.text: Galactose is glucose with one OH flipped: the one on carbon four points up instead of to the side. That's the only difference. Galactose is rarely free in food; it comes as half of milk sugar, lactose. The liver turns it into glucose.

segments.name: Fructose
segments.text: Fructose has the same formula again, C6H12O6, but its C double bond O is on carbon two, so it closes into a five-sided ring. It's the sweetest natural sugar, found in fruit and honey. This one is drawn flat, showing every atom but not which way each OH points.

segments.name: How Fructose Is Handled
segments.text: Fructose is absorbed more slowly than glucose and handled mainly by the liver, which turns most of it into glucose, glycogen, lactate or fat. In whole fruit it comes with fiber and water. Large amounts as added sugar are linked to fatty liver and higher blood fats.

figures.title: The Double Sugars
figures.subtitle: Two single sugars joined by a glycosidic bond.

segments.name: The Glycosidic Bond
segments.text: Two single sugars join through an oxygen bridge called a glycosidic bond. As with the peptide bond, a water molecule is released when it forms, and added back when it's digested. Here, in maltose, carbon one of the first glucose, with its alpha OH pointing down, links to carbon four of the second. That's an alpha one-to-four link, the same one that holds starch together.

segments.name: Sucrose
segments.text: Sucrose, table sugar, is glucose joined to fructose. Both reactive carbons are used in the link. It's naturally in fruit, carrots and beets, and maple sap, and refined from sugar cane and beets. The enzyme sucrase on the gut wall splits it apart.

segments.name: Lactose
segments.text: Lactose, milk sugar, is galactose joined to glucose, but this time with a beta link: the bridge runs out level with the rings. Lactase, an enzyme on the gut wall, splits it. Babies make plenty of lactase; most adults worldwide make much less after childhood.

segments.name: Lactose Intolerance
segments.text: If lactase is low, lactose reaches the colon, where bacteria ferment it into gas, causing bloating, cramps and loose stools. That's lactose intolerance. Yogurt and hard cheeses have much of their lactose already used up by bacteria, so they're often fine.

figures.title: Starch and Glycogen
figures.subtitle: Long glucose chains: how plants and you store fuel.

segments.name: Amylose
segments.text: Starch is how plants store glucose. Amylose is a single long chain, hundreds to thousands of glucoses, all joined by alpha one-to-four links. The alpha link puts a slight turn in each step, so the chain coils into a helix. Each hexagon in these cartoons stands for one glucose ring.

segments.name: Amylopectin
segments.text: Amylopectin is the same chain with branches. Every twenty to thirty glucoses, a new chain starts from carbon six, an alpha one-to-six link. Most starch is about three quarters amylopectin and a quarter amylose.

segments.name: Glycogen
segments.text: Animals, including you, store glucose as glycogen. It's like amylopectin but much more branched, every eight to twelve glucoses, built around a protein core. All those branch ends mean enzymes can release lots of glucose at once when you need it.

segments.name: Cooking Starch
segments.text: Cooking changes starch. Heat and water make starch granules swell and burst, which is why rice softens and gravy thickens, and it makes starch much easier to digest. When cooked starch cools, some chains line up again into resistant starch, which acts like fiber. You'll find starch in grains, potatoes, beans, lentils and green bananas.

figures.title: Fiber
figures.subtitle: Beta links you can’t digest, and the bacteria that can.

segments.name: Alpha Versus Beta
segments.text: Here are two glucoses joined two ways, at the same scale. Maltose has an alpha link, like starch. Cellobiose has a beta link, like cellulose. Same atoms, same formula; only the direction of one bond differs. Your enzymes fit the alpha shape and cut it, but no human enzyme can cut the beta link between two glucoses. Lactase only fits galactose’s beta link, in lactose.

segments.name: Cellulose
segments.text: So cellulose, the main material of plant cell walls, passes through you undigested. Its beta links keep each chain straight, so chains pack side by side and lock together with hydrogen bonds, making strong fibers. Cows and termites only digest it because microbes in their guts can.

segments.name: Soluble and Insoluble
segments.text: Fiber comes in two broad kinds. Soluble fiber, like the beta-glucan in oats and the pectin in apples, dissolves into a gel; it slows digestion and helps lower LDL cholesterol. Insoluble fiber, like the cellulose in bran and vegetable skins, holds water and adds bulk, helping food move through. Resistant starch behaves much like soluble fiber.

segments.name: Food for Bacteria
segments.text: In your colon, bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids: acetate, propionate and butyrate, this small molecule. Butyrate is the main fuel of the cells lining your colon. That's how fiber still gives about two calories per gram.

segments.name: How Much Fiber
segments.text: The US target is fourteen grams of fiber for every thousand calories, about twenty-five grams a day for women and thirty-eight for men under fifty, and most people get about half that. Too little is linked to constipation and, over the long term, more heart disease, type 2 diabetes and colon cancer. Too much too fast causes gas, so increase it slowly and drink enough water.

figures.title: Digestion and Blood Sugar
figures.subtitle: Cut down to single sugars, absorbed, and kept in balance.

segments.name: In the Mouth
segments.text: Carbohydrate digestion starts in your mouth: amylase in saliva begins cutting starch into shorter pieces. That's why bread starts to taste sweet if you chew it long enough. In the stomach, acid stops the amylase.

segments.name: In the Small Intestine
segments.text: In the small intestine, amylase from the pancreas cuts starch down to maltose, and enzymes on the gut wall, maltase, sucrase and lactase, split the double sugars. Only single sugars can be absorbed. They go to the liver first. Fiber and resistant starch carry on to the colon.
segments.cue: Small intestine, Into the blood, Colon

segments.name: Insulin
segments.text: After a meal, blood glucose rises. The pancreas releases insulin, which lets muscle, fat and liver cells take glucose in. Extra glucose is stored as glycogen, and beyond that, as fat.

segments.name: Glucagon
segments.text: Between meals, as glucose falls, the pancreas releases glucagon, and the liver breaks down its glycogen to send glucose back into the blood. Your liver holds roughly a hundred grams of glycogen; your muscles hold a few hundred grams more, but only for their own use.

segments.name: Glycemic Index and Needs
segments.text: The glycemic index compares how fast a food raises blood glucose with pure glucose. Fiber, fat, protein and intact grains slow it down. The US recommended amount of carbohydrate for adults is a hundred and thirty grams a day, based on the brain's glucose use, and the acceptable range is forty-five to sixty-five percent of calories.

figures.title: Sugars on the Label
figures.subtitle: Total sugars, added sugars and sugar alcohols.

segments.name: Sugars in Whole Foods
segments.text: Plenty of whole foods contain sugar. Fruit has fructose, glucose and sucrose; milk has lactose; sweet vegetables and sprouted grains have their own. In whole foods, sugars come packaged with fiber, water, vitamins and minerals.

segments.name: Total and Added Sugars
segments.text: On the label, total sugars counts every single and double sugar, whether it grew in the food or was added. The added sugars line counts only what was put in, including honey, syrups and concentrated juice. Its Daily Value is fifty grams, and the Dietary Guidelines advise keeping added sugars under ten percent of calories.

segments.name: Sugar Alcohols
segments.text: Sugar alcohols, or polyols, are sugars whose C double bond O has gained two hydrogens. Here glucose becomes sorbitol: now every carbon carries an OH. They're only partly absorbed, so they give fewer calories, raise blood glucose less, and don't cause cavities. They're counted in total carbohydrate, not in sugars.

segments.name: Sorbitol
segments.text: Sorbitol is found naturally in prunes, pears, apples and stone fruit. In large amounts it draws water into the gut and ferments, causing gas and diarrhea, which is part of why prunes have their reputation.

figures.title: Where carbohydrates are used in the body
figures.subtitle: Tap a number on the cell to see what that part does; the list below it gives every other place in the body.

segments.name: Where Carbohydrates Go
segments.text: Here's where carbohydrates are used: first inside a single cell, then everywhere else in the body. Starch and sugars are digested to glucose, the body's everyday fuel. Some is stored as glycogen, and fiber goes on to the large intestine.
segments.cue: The cell drawing and the list of places

segments.name: Inside a Cell
segments.text: Glucose enters through carrier proteins in the membrane. In the cytosol, glycolysis splits it in two, and the mitochondria burn the pieces to make most of the cell's ATP. Glucose you don't need right away is linked into glycogen granules for later. And sugars aren't just fuel: the ER and Golgi stick sugar chains onto proteins, giving the cell its outer coat.
segments.cue: The cell drawing and its numbered parts

foodBody.name: Starch
foodBody.text: From grains, potatoes and beans; digested to glucose. Glycogen is the animal version of the same idea.

foodBody.name: Fiber
foodBody.text: Not digested by your cells; gut bacteria ferment some of it into short-chain fatty acids that colon cells burn for fuel.

foodBody.name: Fructose
foodBody.text: From fruit and table sugar; handled mostly by liver cells, which turn it into glucose, glycogen or fat.

segments.name: Glucose as Fuel
segments.text: The brain burns about 120 grams of glucose a day, and red blood cells have no mitochondria, so glucose is all they can use. The pancreas keeps blood sugar in range, releasing insulin when it rises and glucagon when it falls.
segments.cue: In the list: brain, red blood cells and pancreas

foodBody.name: Glucose
foodBody.text: Starch in bread, rice, potatoes and pasta is all glucose, and table sugar is half glucose. In your body it is the main fuel of the brain and the only fuel of red blood cells.

segments.name: Glycogen Stores
segments.text: The liver stores about 100 grams of glycogen and breaks it down to keep blood sugar steady between meals. Muscles hold about 400 grams in total, but keep it for themselves during exercise. In a fast, the liver and kidneys also make new glucose.
segments.cue: In the list: liver, muscle and kidneys

foodBody.name: Glycogen
foodBody.text: There is almost none in food, because it breaks down after slaughter. Your body builds it from glucose and stores it in the liver and muscles.

segments.name: Fiber and the Rest
segments.text: Fiber you can't digest reaches the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it into short-chain fatty acids that feed the cells of the colon wall. In the mouth, saliva starts digesting starch, and bacteria on the teeth turn sugar into the acid that causes cavities. Joint cartilage is built around long sugar chains that hold water.
segments.cue: In the list: large intestine, mouth and joint cartilage

foodBody.name: Short-chain fatty acids
foodBody.text: Not eaten as such: gut bacteria make them, mainly acetate, propionate and butyrate, from fiber in beans, oats and whole grains. Butyrate is the main fuel of the colon wall.

segments.name: Simplified
segments.text: This is simplified. Almost every cell can burn glucose, so the list gives the places that depend on it most or store it, and each one's main job. Glycogen amounts are typical adult values and vary with diet and exercise.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here's every carbohydrate in this lesson in one table: what it's made of, the bond that holds it, whether you can digest it, and where you find it. Notice how much depends on the bond: starch and cellulose are both just glucose.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. Brown, raw and white sugar are all almost entirely sucrose. Honey is mostly free fructose and glucose, and shouldn't be given to babies under one. Whole grains keep the bran and germ, with their fiber, vitamins and minerals; refined grains are mostly starch. And bread tastes sweet as you chew because amylase is already making maltose.
